correctness.rationale: For equal-sum x majorizing y and concave nondecreasing positive f, Karamata gives sum f(x)<=sum f(y), while extreme coordinates give f(x_n)-f(x_1)>=f(y_n)-f(y_1). The Gini numerator for n=2 is the extreme gap, and for n=3 is twice the gap; n=1 is zero. Therefore the Gini ranking is preserved for all n<=3, all positive real profiles satisfying the hypotheses, and every such f. The exact n=4 majorization witness x=(1,1,1,3), y=(1,1,2,2) reverses after cap at 2: 3/20<1/6; independently the smooth positive strictly increasing strictly concave f(t)=1-8^(-t) yields 27/1060<1/34. Exact Fraction verification uses both Gini formulas. No finite experiment is used as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The assessed claim combines a universal three-household common-concave-transform Gini-ranking guarantee with a sharp four-household reversal, including a strictly concave smooth witness. Fellman (2016) gives transformation-to-original and two-transforms-of-one-population Lorenz comparisons, not the two-population common-transform rank comparison; Larrimore et al. (2008) studies survey top-coding estimates, not a finite minimum; Bishop et al. (1994) describes empirical ordinal Lorenz effects in its accessible abstract. Published mathematical-result semantic searches did not find this statement or a visibly stronger theorem, but absence of a hit is not priority proof. The inaccessible 1994 full text leaves a nonzero residual risk.

value.rationale: Income data top-coding and progressive concave transformations are motivated by long-recognized empirical distortions in relative inequality comparisons (1994 and 2008 studies). The result establishes a sharp structural boundary that rules out such Gini-rank reversals under majorization for at most three equally weighted households and shows possibility already with four; strict smooth concavity shows the phenomenon is not an artifact of a flat cap. This exact number of households is intrinsic to the onset of an extra interior Gini weight, and the theorem gives a useful mathematical stress test of ordinal comparisons, without suggesting that real datasets use so few households.
